summary: Andorra has no airport and no visa regime of its own — every visitor arrives by road through France or Spain, so Schengen rules decide who can come: EU/EEA citizens and Schengen visa-free nationalities enter freely, while travelers who need a Schengen visa must carry a multiple-entry one, because entering Andorra means leaving the Schengen Area.

fee.notes: Standard Schengen short-stay visa fee, paid to a French or Spanish consulate — Andorra issues no visas of its own.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

passportValidity.text: Schengen rules apply in practice: your passport should be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure and issued within the last 10 years, since you enter and leave through France or Spain.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

travelInsurance.text: Not checked at the Andorran border, but Schengen visa holders must carry the medical insurance their visa requires (minimum EUR 30,000 cover), and winter-sports cover is strongly recommended for ski trips.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

onwardTicket.text: There are no routine checks at the French and Spanish road borders into Andorra; normal Schengen entry rules apply when you first arrive in Europe.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

proofOfFunds.text: Andorra itself sets no requirement; France or Spain may apply standard Schengen means-of-subsistence checks when you enter the area.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

currencyLimits.text: Cash of EUR 10,000 or more must be declared when entering or leaving the EU through France or Spain, and Andorra applies its own declaration rules for large sums.

source.name: Govern d'Andorra — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

notes: Andorra is outside the EU customs union — duty-free allowances on tobacco, alcohol and fuel are enforced when you drive back into France or Spain, and customs checks with lines are common.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, from ski lifts to the duty-free shopping galleries of Andorra la Vella; cash is rarely needed.

safety.text: Andorra is one of the safest places in Europe, with very little crime. The real risks are alpine ones: winter driving, fast-changing mountain weather and ski injuries.

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to March for skiing in Grandvalira and Pal Arinsal; July and August for hiking, cycling and cool mountain air.

idp.text: Andorra is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Andorra is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Andorra yet.

tips.text: If you needed a visa to enter the Schengen Area, make sure it is multiple-entry before visiting Andorra — driving in counts as leaving Schengen, and a single-entry visa will not get you back into France or Spain.
Andorra has no airport or train station. The usual gateways are Barcelona and Toulouse, around three hours away by road, with regular buses to Andorra la Vella.
Duty-free shopping is a national pastime, but French and Spanish customs enforce strict allowances on tobacco, alcohol and fuel when you leave — exceeding them means fines and confiscation.
In winter, snow chains or winter tires are often mandatory on the mountain roads into Andorra. Check conditions before driving up, especially over the Envalira pass from France.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Andorra?
faq.answer: Andorra issues no visas at all. Entry is governed by Schengen rules because you must pass through France or Spain. EU/EEA citizens and Schengen visa-free nationalities (US, UK, Japan and many more) just drive in; if your passport needs a Schengen visa, get a multiple-entry one so you can re-enter France or Spain afterward.

faq.question: Does time in Andorra count against my 90-day Schengen allowance?
faq.answer: Strictly speaking no — Andorra is outside the Schengen Area. In practice the road borders rarely stamp passports, so keep evidence of your stay (hotel bookings, receipts) if you plan to rely on Andorran days not counting toward the 90/180 limit.

faq.question: Can I visit Andorra on a single-entry Schengen visa?
faq.answer: You would be allowed into Andorra, but your single-entry visa would be used up — France and Spain can refuse to let you back into the Schengen Area, leaving you stranded. Only visit with a multiple-entry Schengen visa or a residence permit.

faq.question: How do I get to Andorra without an airport?
faq.answer: By road. Regular direct buses run from Barcelona and Toulouse airports (about three hours), or you can drive — from Spain via La Seu d'Urgell or from France over the Envalira pass, which can require winter equipment in snow season.

faq.question: What currency does Andorra use?
faq.answer: The euro, under a monetary agreement with the EU — even though Andorra is not an EU member. Cards are accepted almost everywhere.
